newsitem.title: USA: Smoking song, nicknames recalled at Reynolds trial.
newsitem.headline: Smoking song, nicknames recalled at Reynolds trial.

text.p: An expert witness for R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. played a recording of an old Tex Williams song and recalled cigarette nicknames like "coffin nails" on Tuesday to show that the health risks of smoking have been part of common public knowledge for a long time.
Reynolds lawyers said they expected to rest their case Wednesday and closing arguments in the widely watched trial were tentatively slated for Friday.

Using a multimedia presentation that included snippets of old news broadcasts and the 1947 Williams song "Smoke, Smoke, Smoke That Cigarette," University of South Carolina historian Lacy Ford told jurors in a wrongful death trial that there was substantial publicity on the possible links between smoking and illness from the 1900s through the 1960s.

Lawyers for Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., appeared to be using the testimony to bolster their claim that the late Jean Connor chose to smoke despite knowing the possible health risks.

Connor, who smoked from the time she was a teenager and eventually developed a three-pack-a-day habit, died of lung cancer at age 49. Her sister, Dana Raulerson, sued Reynolds for wrongful death on behalf of Connor's estate and her three children.

The smoking song, written in 1947 by Merle Travis for Tex Williams and later popularised by the group Commander Cody and the Lost Planet Airmen, includes the lyrics "puff, puff, puff until you smoke yourself to death," and "nicotine slaves are all the same, at a petting party or a poker game."
Williams, who was a heavy smoker, died in 1985 following a year-long battle with cancer.
Ford said he had researched the history of "common knowledge" about cigarette smoking by combing old magazines, newspapers, television shows and curricula from Jacksonville public schools.

He said that from the turn of the century until the 1950s, cigarettes were referred to as "coffin nails," "cancer sticks" and "little white slavers" and the term "nic-fit" was used to describe the alleged habit-forming nature of the product.

Defence lawyers played a segment of a CBS News report on the 1964 U.S. Surgeon-General's report that linked smoking with lung ailments. In it, moderator Harry Reasoner said, "If you smoke cigarettes, you increase your chances of dying early."
"This was really just saturation coverage" of the Surgeon-General's report, Ford said, comparing the media reporting to that of the O.J. Simpson murder saga.
He said the public was aware not only of the possible health risk, but also of the allegedly addictive nature of cigarettes.
There was a "broad public awareness amounting to common knowledge of those facts for a very long time," Ford said.

Ford, who said he did not read medical journals or internal tobacco company documents to form his perceptions on common knowledge about smoking, cited a 1954 Gallup Poll in which 90 percent of those questioned had heard or read that smoking may cause lung cancer.
At a conference following the testimony, Reynolds lawyers said they expected to call their final witness Wednesday.
Judge Bernard Nachman said rebuttal witnesses could be called Thursday, followed by a conference of lawyers to decide on the instructions to be given to the jury.

Closing arguments could then be given Friday morning with jury deliberations following. Each side was to be given two hours for closing statements, Nachman said. The schedule was tentative, depending on the length of testimony of the final Reynolds' witness, rebuttal and legal arguments to follow.
